chapter_theme: Forbearance carried beyond insult into friendship and privation: avoid fools, bear inferiors, value a friend's harsh words, bear with or quietly leave an erring friend, starve rather than beg from the graceless, and refuse blameworthy pleasure, harm and falsehood even at the greatest cost.
structure_note: Several quatrains address a chieftain of the hills, forest or shore (71, 73, 76, 77, 79), which Mudaliar calls ஆடூஉ முன்னிலை. 71 to 73 concern speech, 75 to 77 friendship, and 78 to 80 holding firm under want.

71.reading: Lord of the good cool hill country where streams fall like garlands: say nothing at all to a fool, who will twist what you say; slipping away as best you can is best.
71.nuance: Forbearance here takes the form of withdrawal rather than endurance: the wise don't stay to bear the fool's talk.

72.reading: When those not one's equals say unfit things, it is fitting to bear them in silence; the world does not count the opposite as praise but as disgrace.
72.nuance: Mudaliar takes the 'world' that judges to be the worthy, not people at large.

73.reading: Lord of the cool shore of the teeming sea, where bees hum over every flower: for one who finds people who know what is good for him, are harsh words from those who love worse than pleasant words that strangers speak with a smile?
73.nuance: The condition carries the weight: harsh words are worth more only if one finds friends who know what is good (ஆவது அறிவார்). Mudaliar reads பெறின் as stressing how rare such friends are.

74.reading: Those who know what must be known, keep restraint, fear what must be feared, do what is due so that the world rejoices, and live content with what they get, are hardly ever in suffering.
74.nuance: Mudaliar glosses அடங்கி as 'being forbearing', which ties this broad portrait of contentment to the chapter's theme.

75.reading: When two have joined in friendship without any distinction and one of them shows conduct the other cannot make sense of, the other should bear it as far as he can, and if he can't, should withdraw without spreading it abroad.

positions.position: The friend's lapse is an act done unknowingly, or one that can't be told to others.
positions.quote: தேற்றா ஒழுக்கம் - அறியாச் செய்கை; (பிறர்க்கு) அறிவிக்கக் கூடாச்செய்கை எனினுமாம்.

positions.position: The friend is found in bad conduct.

76.reading: Lord of the forest land: even if friends do hurtful things, wish them to pass as if pleasant and blame only yourself, but do not abandon those joined to you closely, for parting is hard even for beasts.
76.nuance: Blaming oneself is left open: Mudaliar records two readings, one moral and one karmic.

positions.position: One blames oneself either for the bad deeds of a former birth that caused the hurt, or for befriending without first examining the friend.
positions.quote: (அச் செய்கைக்குக் காரணமாகிய தீ வினையை முற்பிறப்பிற் செய்த) தன்னையே எனவும், (முன் நன்கு ஆராயாது அவரொடு நட்புகொண்ட) தன்னையே எனவும் பொருள் கூறுப.

77.reading: Is it not because the great bear with faults that are hard to bear that people seek their deep friendship? Lord of the good high hills with roaring falls, are close friends rare for those who do good?
77.nuance: The closing question can be taken two ways: Mudaliar reads it as 'friends are not rare for the good', Shanmuganar as 'the great are not hard to win for those who do good without fault'.

78.reading: Even if wasted and starving, do not tell your need to people without courtesy; those who lack the resolve to give up their life tell it only to those able to cover it.
78.nuance: Both commentators take தம்மைத் துறக்கும் துணிவு as resolve to give up one's life, so the quatrain ranks starving in silence above asking even the right person; Pope reads it as resolve to deny oneself. மறைக்கும் can mean relieving the need or keeping it secret, and Mudaliar allows both.

79.reading: Lord of the land of high waterfalls: even if disgrace comes along the way pleasure opened, and even if the pleasure looks as if it would never end, the way that brings no blame comes first.
79.nuance: The second concession is the stronger: not only brief pleasures but lasting ones are to be refused if they carry blame. The first two lines are knotted, and Mudaliar resolves இருந்தைக்க as addressed to the listener.

80.reading: Though ruined, do not plan the ruin of the worthy; though your flesh wastes, do not eat from the hands of those you must not eat from; though you would gain the whole sky-roofed earth, do not speak words mixed with falsehood.
80.nuance: Each refusal is set against the extreme loss that would excuse it, which is how the quatrain belongs to a chapter on forbearance.

positions.position: Those whose food must not be eaten are the guru, the deity and the poor; he records others who say lower castes or those who serve without love.

links.note: Both make getting away from fools a gain: 797 calls leaving a fool's friendship profit, and 71 advises slipping away rather than talking with one.
Both open with the same situation in nearly the same words (நீரல்ல சொல்லியக்கால்): 64 shows the excellent not growing angry, and 72 adds that the world counts retaliation as disgrace.
Both make public regard the measure: 155 says people count those who retaliate as nothing and keep those who forbear like gold, and 72 that the world takes retaliation as disgrace.
784 says friendship exists to rebuke a friend who oversteps, not to laugh together. 73 values those harsh words above an outsider's pleasant ones.
Both use the phrase 'fear what should be feared' (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சு-): 428 makes it the work of the wise, and 74 lists it among the marks of those who live free of suffering.

Adjacent quatrains on a friend who wrongs you: 75 allows quiet withdrawal once one can bear no more, and 76 forbids abandoning a close friend and says to blame oneself. The conflict holds if both concern the same wrong; it weakens if 75's தேற்றா ஒழுக்கம் is the friend's general misconduct rather than hurt done to oneself.
Both forbid broadcasting a close friend's faults with the same verb (தூற்று-): 188 condemns those who spread even their intimates' faults, and 75 says to withdraw without doing so.
Both hold that close friends are not cast off for the harm they do: 807 says those bound by love keep it even when friends bring ruin, and 76 says to blame oneself rather than leave.
Both say that if one must ask, ask only the right people: 1067 pleads with beggars not to ask those who conceal, and 78 forbids telling one's want to the graceless.
1064 praises the worth that won't consent to begging even with nothing left; 78 implies the same ranking, since only those who lack the resolve to die tell their need at all.
Both put blamelessness above the strongest pull: 656 forbids a deed the worthy would blame even to feed one's starving mother, and 79 forbids blameworthy pleasure even if it would never end.
Both refuse to let ruin excuse wrongdoing: 205 says not to do evil because one is poor, and 80 says not to plot the ruin of the worthy even when one is ruined oneself.
